title: Chore Chart for Girls: Free Printable + Editable by Age
meta_description: A free, editable printable chore chart for girls at any age — choose tasks by the kid, not the stereotype. From a dad raising three daughters, 11 to 18.
h1: A Free, Editable Chore Chart for Girls — Built Around the Kid, Not the Cliche
intro: If you searched for a chore chart for girls, you've probably already scrolled past a wall of frilly templates buried under tiaras, cupcakes, and pastel swirls. I want to hand you something different. The chart below is a blank, editable grid you fill in yourself — her tasks down one side, the days across the top — so it bends to your actual daughter instead of some pink idea of what a girl's chart is supposed to be. I'm Andrew, and my wife and I run the SproutChores family. We're raising four kids, three of them girls at eleven, fifteen, and eighteen, with a nine-year-old boy rounding things out, and we've fostered younger children along the way too. So on the specific question of charts for daughters, I'm not working from theory — I've got three of them stretched right across the ages this page covers, and no two have ever needed the same chart. That's really the whole point of what follows. A good chore chart for a girl isn't organized around the fact that she's a girl; it's organized around the real kid standing in front of you. Below I'll walk through why the gendered task lists are safe to ignore, how the chart should shift as she grows from a little one into a teenager, how to let her make it genuinely hers without boxing her into pink, and the single reframe that changed the most for us: treating the chart as a way for you to keep track, not a gadget meant to make her care.

sections.heading: A Chore Chart for Girls Is Still Just a Chore Chart
sections.body:
The gendered chore lists floating around the internet tend to nudge girls toward the same narrow lane — dishes, dusting, tidying, keeping things pretty, helping mom in the kitchen. I'd encourage you to ignore all of that. In our house, two of the three kids who take things apart to figure out how they work happen to be my daughters. My fifteen-year-old is engineering-minded to the core; she needs to understand the mechanism behind everything, and honestly I see a lot of my own childhood in her. My eleven-year-old once spent an entire theme-park ride reverse-engineering how the illusion was built instead of just enjoying the ghosts. Neither of them fits the tidy-and-domestic script, and I'd bet your daughter doesn't either.

So assign tasks by capability and by what adult life will actually demand, never by gender. I think of chores as rehearsal for being a capable grown-up, and the woman your daughter is becoming will need to run a household and handle a toolbox and manage money — none of which belongs to one sex. Put whatever her real life will require on that chart: taking out the trash, yard work, learning to fix a slow drain, cooking a genuine meal, not just wiping counters. The underlying principle holds for every kid; the way you apply it simply bends to the child. A blank, editable grid lets you do exactly that, without a template quietly deciding what a girl is allowed to be responsible for.

sections.heading: How the Chart Should Change From Little Girl to Teen
sections.body:
The single biggest driver of what goes on the chart isn't gender — it's age. With the youngest girls, roughly two to five, the whole job is self-care: getting dressed, brushing teeth, cleaning up their own messes, ideally alongside you since little kids want to copy what a parent does. Somewhere around five or six you can fold in a little shared-space work, but go in expecting to redo it; at that stage you're building the muscle memory and the sense that she's part of a household that leans on everyone, not chasing a spotless bathroom. Through the elementary and tween years the complexity climbs steadily — dishes, helping with cooking, pets, trash, outdoor jobs — and you raise the bar as her skill rises.

The teen years are a different animal, and this is where a lot of parents of teenage girls get stuck. By fifteen or sixteen, capability stopped being the question years ago; she already knows how to run a load of laundry and clean a bathroom properly. What you're actually coaching now is follow-through and holding a real standard without being reminded three times. So for a teen, let the chart read like a plain list of responsibilities rather than a cheerful sticker grid — a fifteen-year-old will tune out anything that looks built for a toddler, and she's not wrong to. Because the grid is editable, you can literally run two different documents under one roof: my eleven-year-old's chart and my teenagers' charts look nothing alike, and that's exactly as it should be.

sections.heading: Let Her Own the Chart (Not Just the Color Pink)
sections.body:
One of the most reliable things I've watched work is handing a kid ownership of the chart itself. My eleven-year-old genuinely lights up when she gets to design and decorate her own, then follow the thing she built — the buy-in comes from making it hers, not from anything I say. So give your daughter the blank grid and let her choose the look: the colors, the layout, whether there's an animal or a character in the corner. If she wants it pink, wonderful. The problem was never the color pink; the problem is pink handed to a girl as the only option she's offered. Let her land on whatever is actually hers.

A quick reality check, though, so you don't set yourself up for disappointment: letting her design it makes her more invested, but it doesn't guarantee she'll love using it forever, and that's fine. Same house, opposite wiring — my son more or less ignores charts as a concept while his sister decorates hers for fun. That gap is about how each kid is built, not about being a boy or a girl. Meet the daughter in front of you where she actually is, expect to adjust, and treat a chart that stops landing as a signal to tweak it rather than proof that charts don't work for her.

sections.heading: The Chart Is Your Dashboard, Not Her Bribe
sections.body:
Here's the reframe that changed the most for us. The chart's real job is to let me see how each kid is doing so I know when to step in — it is a tracking tool for the parent, not a machine engineered to manufacture motivation in the child. The motivation itself comes from a plain, steady expectation that everyone under this roof carries a share of the load, because that's simply what being part of a family costs. A grid of boxes can't install that; the family culture does.

That means keeping a few lanes deliberately separate. We don't make our kids buy screen time by doing chores, and we don't claw back money as a penalty for unrelated misbehavior. Allowance exists in our house, but it rides on the whole picture — whether the work held up, whether she stayed dependable without being chased, and the attitude she brought to it — never a price stapled to each box. Two more things earn their keep here. Advance notice is a nearly free way to kill conflict: 'in about an hour we're going to unload the dishwasher' lands far better than 'do it right now,' because it gives her a beat to get her head around it. And with an older girl, resist the urge to over-rescue. My fifteen-year-old once let something important slide, waved off the help I offered, and ended up missing an event she'd really wanted to attend. It stung to let that consequence stand, but the next time around she sorted it out on her own — which no lecture from me was ever going to accomplish.

faq.q: What chores should a teenage girl be responsible for?
faq.a: By the teen years, the honest answer is: just about anything in the house, and none of it is gendered. A thirteen-to-eighteen-year-old can cook a real meal, run her own laundry start to finish, handle dishes and trash, keep shared spaces livable, look after pets, and pitch in on bigger weekend projects, indoors and out. Capability stopped being the question a while ago. What you're really coaching at this age is doing the job to a real standard and finishing it without a second reminder. Because the chart here is a blank editable grid, you set the tasks at her level and raise the bar as she proves she can carry more — and you keep the wording plain and grown-up so it reads like a list of responsibilities rather than something built for a small child.

faq.q: Should a chore chart for a girl be different from one for a boy?
faq.a: In our experience, no. The tasks should be chosen for the individual kid — her age, her skill, what her adult life will actually require — not for her being a girl. I've got three daughters and a son, and if anything the stereotype gets it backwards in our house: my girls are the ones drawn to how things work and happy to tackle yard work and repairs, while my nine-year-old boy is the one who now gathers all the household trash on his own. Assign chores by the person in front of you, not by a pink-versus-blue script. A blank, editable chart is genuinely better for exactly this reason — nothing on it decides in advance what a girl is or isn't supposed to handle.

faq.q: What age should a girl start doing chores?
faq.a: Earlier than most people think, as long as you match the expectation to the age. From about two to five, 'chores' really means self-care she does herself — getting dressed, brushing teeth, cleaning up her own messes — often done right alongside you, since little kids love copying a parent. Around five or six you can add small shared-space jobs, but treat that stage as building the habit and the sense of belonging to a household, not as getting the work done well; you'll be redoing plenty of it, and that's normal. From there the responsibilities grow steadily with her skill. The goal isn't a spotless house at age six. It's a girl who, years down the road, can carry a job from start to finish on her own.
